is important to note that 50 g of available carbohydrate is rarely the same as 50 g of food and may not reﬂect amounts of food
normally ingested. For example, USDA nutrient database shows that 28 g of beets contain 2.7 g of carbohydrate and 1.9 g of avail-
able carbohydrate, so 50 g of available carbohydrate from beets, the test amount eaten, is 0.72 kg or 5–6 medium beets).
Some argue that GI is similar to values in tables for nutrients. While similarities exist, there are important differences. First, the
nutrients are determined by precise chemical analyses, but GI is a physiological measure that averages data from 10 human subjects,
who have followed rigid diet and exercise protocols for 3 days prior to the test and ingest 50 g of available carbohydrate food after
fasting. The blood glucose response is monitored for 2 h, and this is repeated on 3 separate occasions. The resulting AUCs are
compared to each subject’s own standard. Despite the strict protocols, variability within and among subjects is high (DeVries,
2008; Matthan et al., 2016). The application of data, collected on a single food after a strict protocol, to situations where foods
